items.prose: `Quote` keeps `bid_ < ask_` as an invariant. Four drafts of `set_ask`:
items.question: Which draft keeps the invariant?

options.text: `void set_ask(double a) { if (a <= bid_) throw std::invalid_argument(""); ask_ = a; }`
`void set_ask(double a) { ask_ = a; if (ask_ <= bid_) std::cout << "crossed"; }`
options.why: It stores first and only prints. The quote is left crossed.
It skips the check, so any ask goes in, even one below the bid.

options.text: `void set_ask(double a) { if (a >= bid_) throw std::invalid_argument(""); ask_ = a; }`
options.why: The test is the wrong way round: it refuses every valid ask and accepts every crossed one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The ask must stay above the bid, checked before it is stored.

explain.text: A changing function checks before it stores, so a refused call leaves the object as it was. An ask equal to the bid is refused too, as in the lesson.

items.question: Put the output in order.

feedback.correct: Members first, then the body; on the way out, the reverse.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Members are built before the constructor's body runs, and destroyed after the destructor's body.

byKey.do: The constructor's body runs only after every member has been built.
byKey.cf: Members are destroyed in reverse declaration order: `risk_` before `feed_`.
byKey.dc: The destructor's body runs first; the members it may use are destroyed after it.

explain.text: The members are built in declaration order before the body prints `desk open`. Destruction mirrors it: the body prints `desk close`, then `risk_` and `feed_` close, newest first.

items.prose: You want `std::cout << q` to print a `Quote`, and to chain with more `<<`.
items.question: Which declaration do you write?

options.why: Streams cannot be copied, so neither the parameter nor the return can be by value.
As a member, the `Quote` would be the left operand: you would have to write `q << std::cout`.
It prints once, but returns nothing for the next `<<` in a chain.

feedback.correct: Stream by reference in, the same stream out.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The stream must be on the left, by reference, and returned.

explain.text: A free function puts the stream on the left. Taking and returning `std::ostream&` passes the one stream along the chain.

items.question: How many functions does the compiler write from the `max_of` template?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count types, not calls.

byKey.calls: You counted calls. Calls with the same type share one function.
byKey.one: Each type used gets its own function.

explain.text: `int` and `std::string` are each used twice, `double` once: three instantiations, written at compile time.

items.prose: A desk's risk limit caps the absolute exposure, long or short. A negative limit makes no sense, so it can never be set.
items.question: Finish `RiskLimit`: refuse a negative limit in the constructor and in `set`, and write `allows`, true when $|\text{exposure}| \le$ the limit.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 9 hidden tests; two pass only if the program stops.

feedback.correct: The limit can never go negative, through either door.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

explain.text: The constructor and `set` both refuse a negative value, so no `RiskLimit` ever holds one. `allows` checks both sides: a short of £6m breaks a £5m limit as surely as a long.

items.prose: Money now carries its currency. Adding pounds to dollars is a bug, so `+` refuses it. Two amounts are equal only when both pence and currency match.
items.question: Write `Money operator+(const Money& a, const Money& b)` and `bool operator==(const Money& a, const Money& b)`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 7 hidden tests; adding GBP to USD must stop the program.

feedback.correct: Mixed currencies are refused, never silently added.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

explain.text: `+` checks the currencies before adding, so £1 plus one dollar stops the program instead of giving 200 pence of nothing. `==` compares both fields, so `<` would need both too if you added one.

items.question: Which line compiles?

options.why: The copy constructor is deleted, because `unique_ptr` cannot be copied.
Copy assignment is deleted for the same reason: one lattice cannot have two owners.
A `const` object cannot be moved from, so this asks for the deleted copy.

feedback.correct: A `unique_ptr` member makes the class move-only.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which special members does `unique_ptr` allow?

explain.text: With the rule of zero, `Pricer` gets what its members allow: moves, but no copies. Moving from a `const` object falls back to the copy, which is deleted.

items.prose: A screen ranks values: the `n` largest, largest first. Write it once for any type with `<`.
items.question: Write `template <typename T> std::vector<T> top_n(std::vector<T> xs, int n)`. If `n` is larger than the vector, return all of it, largest first.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 7 hidden tests with vectors of `int`, `double` and `std::string`.

feedback.correct: One template ranks numbers and tickers alike.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

explain.text: `xs` is taken by value, so sorting it leaves the caller's vector alone. `std::sort` then `std::reverse` puts the largest first, and `resize` keeps `n`, only when `n` is smaller.

items.prose: On the bid side, the highest price trades first, and at the same price the earliest order. `Order` has `long long price` and `int time` (1 came first).
items.question: Which body of `operator<(const Order& a, const Order& b)` puts bids in trading order?

options.why: That flips time as well, so at one price the latest order trades first.
That is the ask side: lowest price first.
It ignores time, so orders at one price come out in any order.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Flip the price comparison only.

explain.text: Putting `b.price` on the left flips the price order, highest first, while `a.time` on the left keeps earlier times first. Tuples compare the price and look at time only on a tie.
